question: A mother gave birth to a newborn two weeks ago. She started seeing blood little by little on her body. However, as the days went by, she noticed that something like the stomach and blood were coming out. Sometimes the mother of the child is different, and she has a neck that is not good. What are the steps that the mother needs to take to prevent this disease?
model_answer:
This is not something to downplay: increasing bleeding 2 weeks after delivery, passage of clots or “flesh/tissue,” foul-smelling discharge, and lower abdominal pain can be due to retained placenta/products, infection of the womb (postpartum endometritis/puerperal sepsis), or delayed postpartum bleeding.  
Lower abdominal pain with fever, weakness, bad-smelling vaginal discharge, or heavy bleeding is a danger sign of disease and she should go to a hospital urgently for examination, scan, blood tests, and treatment such as antibiotics or removal of retained tissue if present.  
Other danger signs after childbirth include soaking pads with blood, dizziness/fainting, severe headache or blurred vision, convulsions, chest pain/breathlessness, painful swollen leg, painful breast with fever, or wound swelling/pus.  
To reduce risk, deliver with a skilled attendant, keep the perineal area clean, change sanitary pads often, wash hands, do not insert herbs/cloths/fingers into the vagina, avoid sex until bleeding stops and she is healed, and attend postnatal checks.  
If any of these signs are present, she should not wait at home because postpartum infection and bleeding can become life-threatening quickly.

question: My name is Mrs Akinleyeg. For about the past two months, I have noticed that my husband's breathing has not been normal at all. He also sneezes repeatedly, especially whenever he is in a dusty environment or in a place where something is being fried. He sneezes repeatedly and finds it difficult to breathe properly. His breathing becomes labored and he tends to sneeze whenever he's in places with smoke or dust. Is there any test that can be carried? out to determine exactly what is causing these symptoms, could staying in dusty places be the cause, or is his body system changing in a way that is making this happen, what type of medication can he use so that his breathing will become normal and comfortable at all times, wherever he may be.
reference:
My name is Mrs. Akinleye. For about the past two months, I have noticed that my husband's breathing has not been normal at all. He also sneezes repeatedly, especially whenever he is in a dusty environment or in a place where something is being fried. He sneezes repeatedly and finds it difficult to breathe properly.

His breathing becomes laboured, and he tends to sneeze whenever he is in places with smoke or dust.

Is there any test that can be carried out to determine exactly what is causing these symptoms? Could staying in dusty places be the cause, or is his body's system changing in a way that is making this happen? What type of medication can he use so that his breathing will become normal and comfortable at all times, wherever he may be?
model_answer:
Mrs Akinleyeg, his symptoms strongly suggest allergy-related rhinitis with possible asthma or airway irritation, commonly triggered by dust, smoke, frying fumes, perfumes, cold air, or mould.  
He should see a doctor for examination and tests such as spirometry or peak-flow testing before and after salbutamol, oxygen level check, chest X-ray if needed, and possibly allergy testing to identify triggers.  
Dusty or smoky places can definitely cause or worsen this, but new adult-onset asthma, infection, heart disease, or chronic lung disease must also be ruled out.  
Treatment may include avoiding triggers, using a face mask in dusty areas, improving ventilation, and medicines such as a non-sedating antihistamine, nasal steroid spray, and if asthma is confirmed, prescribed inhalers such as salbutamol and an inhaled steroid controller.  
If he has severe breathlessness, chest pain, bluish lips, cannot speak full sentences, or symptoms at night, take him to the hospital urgently.

model_answer:
Yes, these are serious danger signs: at about 6 months, severe abdominal/back pain with watery fluid and bleeding may mean preterm labour, rupture of membranes, miscarriage, or bleeding problems like placental abruption/placenta previa.  
She should not be managed at home or just sent casually for a scan; she must go immediately to a hospital with maternity/emergency obstetric care.  
An ultrasound scan is useful, but it should be done after urgent clinical assessment, and no untrained person should put fingers into the vagina because bleeding from placenta previa can worsen.  
At the hospital they will check her vital signs, baby’s heartbeat, whether the “water” is amniotic fluid, the placenta position, and decide on treatment such as admission, antibiotics, steroid injections for baby’s lungs, or delivery if mother or baby is in danger.  
Please refer her urgently now, especially because she is bleeding and leaking water before her due date.

model_answer:
Yes, many causes of chronic cough and breathing difficulty in a 1-year-old can be treated or well controlled, but Meju needs proper hospital assessment urgently, especially because it started soon after birth and affects breathing.  
It may be asthma or reactive airway disease, but cough from early infancy can also be due to congenital airway/lung or heart problems, recurrent infection, aspiration/reflux, tuberculosis exposure, or allergy, so a doctor should examine her and may request oxygen check, chest X-ray, and other tests.  
Stop herbal mixtures, as they may worsen breathing or damage the liver/kidneys and delay correct treatment.  
To reduce attacks, avoid smoke from firewood/charcoal/kerosene and cigarettes, dust, mould, strong perfumes/insecticides, cold air, animal hair, cockroaches, and keep the room well ventilated and clean.  
Go to hospital immediately if she is breathing fast, chest is drawing in, lips look blue, she cannot feed, becomes weak, or has fever.

A 7-day-old baby who is not sucking well and sounds blocked in the nose needs to be seen urgently at a hospital/paediatric clinic today, because poor feeding in a newborn can be a danger sign of infection, breathing difficulty, low blood sugar, jaundice, or dehydration.  
Newborn babies breathe mostly through the nose, so even simple mucus/catarrh can make them struggle to breastfeed, but the sleepiness and poor sucking make it more serious and should not be managed at home alone.  
It is unlikely to be “water entering the head”; more common causes are nasal blockage with mucus, newborn infection, or breathing problems after birth.  
While going to hospital, you can put normal saline nose drops and gently clear the nose before feeds, keep the baby warm, and try small frequent breastfeeding, but do not give herbal mixtures, antibiotics, or cold medicines unless prescribed.  
Go immediately, especially if there is fever or low temperature, fast breathing, chest indrawing, blue lips, yellow eyes/skin, fewer wet nappies, or the baby is too weak to wake and suck.

question: Doctor, a mother living in our house began to notice that her baby was not breastfeeding well. Whenever she tried to breastfeed the baby, the baby would suck for a little while and then stop as if exhausted. The mother also noticed that the baby did not have enough strength to breastfeed and would sweat heavily on the head and face. Not only that, the baby's breathing changed. It seems as though the baby was breathing upward and downward like someone struggling to breathe. As the days went by, the mother became increasingly worried. She wondered whether it was because the baby was not feeding enough or whether there was a problem related to the baby's breathing and sweating. Therefore, she decided to go to the hospital to see a doctor for an examination of the baby. My question is, what could cause a baby? to have difficulty breastfeeding properly. Is the way the baby is breathing a sign of any health problem? What danger signs should the baby's parents watch out for? What could cause a young child to sweat while breastfeeding?
reference:
Doctor, a mother living in our house began to notice that her baby was not breastfeeding well. Whenever she tried to breastfeed the baby, the baby would suck for a little while and then stop as if exhausted.
The mother also noticed that the baby did not have enough strength to breastfeed and would sweat heavily on the head and face. Not only that, the baby's breathing changed; it seemed as though the baby was breathing upward and downward, like someone struggling to breathe.
As the days went by, the mother became increasingly worried. She wondered whether it was because the baby was not feeding enough, or whether there was a problem related to the baby's breathing and sweating. Therefore, she decided to go to the hospital to see a doctor for an examination of the baby.
My question is: what could cause a baby to have difficulty breastfeeding properly? Is the way the baby is breathing a sign of any health problem? What danger signs should the baby's parents watch out for? What could cause a young child to sweat while breastfeeding?
model_answer:
A baby who sucks briefly then stops tired, sweats on the head/face during feeds, and breathes with chest “pulling in” or moving up and down may have a serious problem such as congenital heart disease with heart failure, pneumonia/bronchiolitis, severe infection, anaemia, or another breathing/airway problem.  
Yes, that type of breathing can be a danger sign, especially if there is fast breathing, chest indrawing, grunting, flaring nostrils, blue lips/tongue, or pauses in breathing.  
Parents should also watch for poor feeding, extreme weakness or sleepiness, fever or low body temperature, convulsions, vomiting everything, reduced urine/wet nappies, poor weight gain, or swelling of the legs/face.  
Sweating while breastfeeding often happens because feeding is “exercise” for the baby, and in conditions like heart failure or lung disease the baby works too hard to breathe and suck at the same time.  
This baby should be taken urgently to a hospital or paediatric emergency unit for examination, oxygen check, chest/heart assessment, and treatment.

question: A mother of a young child became worried about her 8-month-old baby. During the daytime, the baby plays well, but every night the baby starts coughing. model_answer:
Yes—severe night cough with fast or difficult breathing in an 8‑month‑old can be a sign of a chest/lung problem such as bronchiolitis, pneumonia, wheezing/asthma-like illness, croup, whooping cough, or aspiration/reflux, and in Nigeria pneumonia is especially important to rule out.  

Because the baby had fast breathing, struggling to breathe, poor breastfeeding and reduced play, these are danger signs and the child should be taken to a hospital/doctor urgently, especially if there is chest indrawing, noisy breathing, blue lips, fever, convulsions, or unusual sleepiness.  

At home while going for care, keep the baby slightly upright, clear a blocked nose with saline drops and gentle suction, continue breastfeeding in small frequent amounts, keep the room free from smoke/dust/perfume, and use paracetamol only if there is fever.  

Do not give cough syrups, herbal mixtures, leftover antibiotics, or adult medicines to an 8‑month‑old unless prescribed, as they can be harmful and may delay proper treatment.  

The doctor may check the breathing rate, oxygen level and chest, and treatment may include oxygen, nebulization/inhaler, antibiotics if pneumonia is suspected, or other medicines depending on the cause.

question: A woman had a baby, a child, about five months ago. The child should be brought to hospital promptly, because severe crying with arm/leg pain at 5 months may be due to sickle cell painful crisis, infection of bone/joint, fracture/trauma, rickets or other serious conditions.  
At home, keep the baby well fed and hydrated, handle the limbs gently, and you may give infant paracetamol in the correct dose based on the baby’s weight, but avoid herbal mixtures or adult pain medicines.  
The doctor will examine the child and may request tests such as full blood count, Hb genotype, infection tests, calcium/vitamin D levels, and X-rays if needed.  
Also note that most 5-month-old babies do not crawl yet, but they should be moving both arms and legs, reaching, rolling or trying to sit with support.  
Go urgently if there is fever, swelling of hands/feet, refusal to feed, weakness of one limb, excessive sleepiness, or fast breathing.

Severe persistent headache with stiff neck and sudden tiny skin spots/sores is a medical emergency, most concerning for meningitis/meningococcal infection or another serious brain/blood infection, even if fever is not obvious.  
The wife should take him to the nearest hospital/emergency unit immediately or call for ambulance—do not wait at home or treat it as “sleeping on the neck.”  
If he is conscious, keep him lying down, avoid bright light, give only paracetamol for pain/fever if available, and do not give antibiotics, herbal mixtures, or strong painkillers before assessment unless prescribed.  
At the hospital he may need urgent examination, blood tests, lumbar puncture if safe, and immediate injectable antibiotics such as ceftriaxone, because delay can lead to death or brain damage.  
If meningococcal disease is confirmed or strongly suspected, close household contacts may also need preventive antibiotics and public health advice.

question: My daughter is pregnant. She is about 24 years old. She's the one who is pregnant. This happened today. At night, I noticed that she started having pain. My daughter is pregnant; she is about twenty-four years old. She is the one who is pregnant. This happened today.
At night, I noticed that she started having pain. She had already packed her belongings and came to my house. As the pain continued, I saw that it was increasing. I gathered all her belongings, and she did not initially allow us to go to the hospital.

Or is it possible they will do surgery for her?
model_answer:
Yes, increasing waist/abdominal pain with the cervix opening is usually labour pain, especially in a first pregnancy, and first labour can take many hours as the cervix gradually opens to 10 cm.  
The safest thing is that she remains in the hospital so nurses/doctors can monitor her contractions, blood pressure, bleeding, the baby’s heartbeat, and the progress of the cervix.  
A baby being too big or not fitting through the birth canal can happen, but it is judged by the mother’s pelvis, baby’s position/size, and whether labour is progressing normally.  
If labour is not progressing, the baby’s heartbeat becomes abnormal, there is heavy bleeding, severe high blood pressure, wrong baby position, or obstruction, they may advise Caesarean section to save mother and baby.  
Please encourage her to cooperate with the hospital team, and immediately alert them if she has severe continuous pain, bleeding, convulsions, fever, or reduced baby movement.

This is an emergency: fever with worsening yellow eyes/skin, vomiting, shivering and severe weakness may be severe malaria with jaundice, hepatitis, blood breakdown, or serious infection affecting the liver, and they need hospital treatment now.  
They should be assessed immediately, likely admitted, and have urgent tests: malaria test/blood film, full blood count/PCV, blood sugar, liver function/bilirubin, kidney/electrolytes, urine test, and hepatitis tests; blood culture may be needed.  
Treatment may include IV fluids, medicine to stop vomiting, paracetamol in correct dose, IV antimalarial such as artesunate if severe malaria is suspected/confirmed, antibiotics if bacterial infection is suspected, and blood transfusion if the blood level is low.  
Do not continue herbal mixtures, alcohol, or repeated paracetamol/unknown drugs because they can worsen liver injury.  
Bring them to the emergency unit immediately, especially if they are confused, very weak, not passing urine, bleeding, convulsing, or unable to keep anything down.

question: A newborn baby that has just been delivered in our hospital about 20 minutes ago was found to appear sleepy. The baby did not cry well since being delivered. When we checked its respiration, it was fine, but the baby was asleep all through. We also checked the temperature and it was normal. Here is my question. What could cause a newborn baby to appear as if it is sleeping and not cry properly since it's Birth, also what kind of treatment will be effective for such baby, and when the mother gets home, what could she administer to the child and what she should not, and what kind of food should the mother eat to ensure that both the mother and baby will be healthy?

When we checked it's respiration,  it was fine but the baby was asleep althrough, we also checked the temperature, and it was normal. Here is my question, what could cause a new born baby to appear as if it is sleeping? And not cry properly since it's birth? Also, what kind of treatment will be effective for such baby? And, when the mother gets home, what could she administer to the child and what she should not, and what kind of food should the mother eat to ensure that both the mother and baby will be healthy?
model_answer:
A newborn who is very sleepy and did not cry well after birth may have birth asphyxia, low blood sugar, effects of drugs given to the mother during labour, infection/sepsis, prematurity, or rarely brain injury, so the baby should not be sent home until reviewed by a doctor or paediatrician.  
Effective treatment depends on the cause: keep the baby warm, check oxygen saturation, blood sugar and vital signs, ensure good breathing, start early breastfeeding if the baby can suck, give IV glucose if sugar is low, oxygen/resuscitation if needed, and antibiotics if infection is suspected.  
At home, the mother should give only breast milk for the first 6 months; do not give water, glucose water, herbs, honey, alcohol, antibiotics, or any medicine unless prescribed by a health worker.  
She should return immediately if the baby is too weak to suck, becomes blue, develops fever or low temperature, fast/difficult breathing, convulsions, persistent vomiting, yellow eyes/body, or remains unusually sleepy.

Examine the vagina and cervix with good light and instruments to look for tears and repair them, remove retained tissue manually if trained and safe, and consider ultrasound/palpation to exclude retained placenta or a second baby.

She should go to hospital immediately, where doctors can give safe pain relief, fluids, blood transfusion if needed, medicines or surgery depending on the cause, and treatment to protect the mother and baby.

Because the wound is red and swollen, it may already be infected, so doctors commonly give antibiotics such as amoxicillin-clavulanate, pain relief, and tetanus vaccination/booster with tetanus immunoglobulin if immunization is incomplete or unknown.  
The dog should be confined and observed by veterinary/public health authorities for 10 days, but treatment must not wait; tests are usually not needed to start rabies prevention, though wound culture, blood tests, or X-ray may be done if there is pus, fever, deep injury, or suspected bone/joint involvement.

This is an obstetric emergency; the most likely cause is **placental abruption**—the placenta separates before delivery, causing **severe abdominal pain, heavy bleeding, uterine tenderness/rigidity and danger to mother and baby**.  
She should be managed immediately with **ABC resuscitation**, left lateral position, oxygen, two large IV lines, IV fluids, urgent blood transfusion if needed, catheter, close monitoring of pulse/BP/urine output, and urgent call to the obstetric, anaesthetic and theatre team.  
Investigations include **full blood count, blood group and cross-match, clotting profile, fibrinogen, urea/electrolytes, bedside ultrasound for fetal heartbeat/placenta**, and CTG fetal monitoring if the baby is alive and viable—but treatment must not wait for ultrasound.  
Treatment is **stabilize the mother and deliver the baby urgently**, usually by emergency caesarean section if bleeding is severe or the baby is distressed/alive, with blood products and treatment of any hypertension or clotting problem; give anti-D if she is Rh-negative.  
She should avoid **alcohol, smoking, herbal mixtures, unsafe drugs, undercooked/unpasteurized foods**, and maintain handwashing, clean perineal hygiene, clean pads, no vaginal douching or inserting herbs, and attend antenatal/follow-up care.

model_answer:
His symptoms—excessive thirst, passing large amounts of urine frequently (especially at night), tiredness and blurred vision—are very suggestive of high blood sugar/diabetes mellitus, and he should go to a healthcare facility as soon as possible for testing.  

He needs a random blood sugar immediately, fasting blood sugar, HbA1c, urine test for glucose/ketones/protein, kidney function/electrolytes, blood pressure check, and possibly cholesterol tests; if he is vomiting, very weak, confused, breathing fast, or has very high sugar, he needs urgent/emergency care.  

High blood sugar causes the kidneys to pull excess sugar into the urine, dragging water with it, which leads to frequent large urination, dehydration, thirst, tiredness and blurred vision; other causes can include diabetes insipidus, kidney disease, urinary infection, high calcium, certain drugs, or excessive fluid intake, but diabetes must be ruled out first.  

High blood pressure alone usually does not cause this pattern, though it can coexist with diabetes and damage the kidneys, so it must also be checked.  

Until he is assessed, he should avoid sugary drinks, fruit juices, energy drinks, alcohol, sweets, and large portions of refined carbohydrates like white bread/rice; encourage water, vegetables, beans, whole grains in controlled portions, lean protein, and regular activity, and adults should screen for diabetes at least every 1–3 years—or more often if overweight, hypertensive, or symptomatic like this.

He should see a mental health professional, child psychologist, counsellor, or trained social worker if symptoms are severe, last more than 2–4 weeks, he cannot function, keeps refusing food, has sleep problems, guilt, talks of wanting to die, or behaves strangely.  
Medication is usually not the first treatment for grief in children; counselling, family support and monitoring are most important, while medicines are only used if a doctor diagnoses depression, severe anxiety, sleep disorder, or another condition.  
If he refuses fluids/food for a whole day, becomes very weak, talks about self-harm, or you fear he may harm himself, take him urgently to the hospital.

question: I took my pregnant friend, who is 18 years old, to the hospital because she had gone into labor and her time had come. The baby can survive, especially if she cried and received oxygen quickly, but she needs close monitoring in a newborn unit because poor breathing after delivery may be due to birth asphyxia, infection, fluid in the lungs, prematurity, or effects of prolonged labour.  
Whether she will become disabled depends mainly on how long her brain was short of oxygen, her Apgar scores, cord blood results if available, and whether she develops seizures, poor feeding, abnormal tone, or unconsciousness in the first 24–72 hours.  
Many babies who improve quickly with stimulation and oxygen grow normally, but babies with severe or prolonged birth asphyxia can later develop cerebral palsy, epilepsy, hearing/vision problems, or developmental delay.  
She should remain under doctors’ care for oxygen monitoring, blood sugar checks, temperature control, infection treatment if needed, and observation for seizures or signs of hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy.  
If she starts breathing well, feeds well, has no seizures, and remains alert over the next few days, her chances of normal development are much better.

question: As a brave woman holding her child, seeing that the child is feverish, the child suddenly starts shaking. The child is having convulsions and is no longer in control. What kind of illness is affecting this nursing mother ⁇ s child, and what kind of care can be given to this child?

The child is most likely having a **febrile convulsion (fever-induced seizure)**, commonly triggered by high fever from infections such as **malaria, respiratory infection, ear infection, or sometimes meningitis**.  
Place the child **on the side**, remove nearby dangerous objects, loosen tight clothing, and **do not put anything in the mouth or force the child down**.  
If the convulsion lasts **more than 5 minutes**, repeats, or the child does not wake up well afterward, take the child to the **nearest hospital immediately** for emergency treatment such as diazepam/oxygen if needed.  
After the fit stops, reduce fever with **paracetamol** and tepid sponging, and ensure the child is tested and treated for the cause, especially **malaria**, which is common in Nigeria.  
Any first-time convulsion, very young baby, stiff neck, persistent vomiting, weakness, or poor feeding needs urgent medical assessment to rule out serious infection.

Her withdrawal, loss of interest, poor appetite/social avoidance and persistent tired/unhappy appearance may suggest depression, anxiety, emotional distress, bullying/abuse, substance use, grief, or sometimes a physical illness, so it should be taken seriously and not dismissed as “bad behaviour.”  
Help by speaking to her calmly and privately, listening without blaming, encouraging regular meals/sleep, gentle activity, and reducing pressure while involving a trusted adult she feels safe with.  
She should see a counsellor, psychologist, psychiatrist, or a doctor at a hospital/primary health centre for assessment, especially if symptoms last more than 2 weeks or affect school, eating, sleep, or relationships.  
Warning signs needing urgent help include talking about death or suicide, self-harm, giving away belongings, severe hopelessness, hearing voices, extreme agitation, refusing food/fluids, running away, or signs of abuse.  
If any suicide or self-harm risk is present, do not leave her alone—take her immediately to the nearest emergency unit or mental health service.

question: A 22 year old lady who gave birth at our hospital 3 days ago brought her baby today for routine immunizations. model_answer:
This is an emergency: a 3-day-old baby who is not feeding, very cold, floppy and excessively sleepy likely has serious neonatal illness such as sepsis, hypoglycaemia, hypothermia, dehydration, prematurity/low birth weight problems, or less commonly a metabolic/neurological problem.  

The “freezing cold” body is not just from refusing breast milk; refusal to feed may be a sign of the underlying illness, and the coldness can worsen low blood sugar and shock.  

Check temperature, blood glucose, oxygen saturation and weight immediately, keep the baby skin-to-skin under warm wraps/radiant warmer, and admit urgently for neonatal care with IV 10% dextrose if hypoglycaemic, careful fluids/feeding support, blood cultures if possible, and empiric antibiotics according to local neonatal sepsis protocol.  

Breastfeeding should be supported after stabilization—assess latch, express breast milk, and give by cup/spoon or nasogastric tube if the baby cannot suck safely.  

Do not give routine immunizations today while the baby is severely ill; stabilize and treat first, then give BCG/OPV/Hepatitis B as soon as clinically stable, unless there is a specific contraindication.

model_answer:
This is an emergency: postpartum weakness, dizziness and “dim/blurry” vision soon after delivery should be treated as postpartum haemorrhage/shock until proven otherwise, while also checking blood pressure and blood sugar.  
Do not give food first; lay her flat, call for help, check vital signs, uterine tone, vaginal bleeding/clots, placenta completeness and genital tract tears, and insert two wide-bore IV lines.  
Start IV fluids, give uterotonics such as oxytocin, uterine massage if the uterus is soft, and tranexamic acid if bleeding is suspected, while sending blood for PCV/Hb, grouping and cross-match.  
Give blood transfusion if she is in shock, has heavy/ongoing bleeding, or her Hb/PCV is low—not just because she feels weak, but based on clinical assessment and labs.  
Also check BP urgently because blurred vision can suggest pre-eclampsia/eclampsia; if BP is high or there are danger signs, treat with magnesium sulphate and antihypertensives according to protocol.

question: A 30 year old woman gave birth a few minutes ago. The delivery was said to be normal. However, since the baby was born, the baby has been having serious difficulty. The baby is not crying well and is not responding as a newborn should. After birth, the baby did not cry properly and seems to have difficulty waking up. The body seems stiff or not moving properly as expected. The baby Baby also cannot feed well and is struggling to breastfeed. The mother is worried because her previous children used to cry immediately after birth. What can cause this problem? What tests can be done on the baby and what emergency steps should be taken? model_answer:
This baby may have **birth asphyxia with hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy (HIE)**, meaning the brain and body did not get enough oxygen around delivery; other possible causes include neonatal infection/sepsis, low blood sugar, seizures, birth injury/bleeding in the brain, prematurity, congenital problems, or effects of drugs given to the mother.  
The baby needs **immediate newborn resuscitation**: keep warm, clear the airway if blocked, stimulate, check breathing/heart rate/oxygen level, and give **bag-and-mask ventilation with oxygen** if not breathing well, with urgent transfer to a Special Care Baby Unit/NICU.  
Tests should include **Apgar score review, blood glucose immediately, oxygen saturation, blood gas if available, full blood count, blood culture/CRP, electrolytes/calcium, bilirubin**, and brain assessment such as cranial ultrasound/EEG where available.  
Treatment includes correcting low sugar with IV dextrose, oxygen/ventilation support, IV fluids, antibiotics if infection is possible, seizure control with medicines like phenobarbital, and careful monitoring of temperature, breathing, urine, and feeding.  
If HIE is suspected and the baby is less than 6 hours old, **therapeutic cooling** in a capable centre can reduce brain injury, so the baby should be managed urgently by a paediatric/neonatal team.

question: A caregiver who is taking care of a small child noticed that the child she is caring for is struggling to breathe and the child's breathing is not normal. She also noticed that the child coughs repeatedly and the cough is very severe. The child is not a baby that was abandoned at birth nor a child that is usually bathed with cold water. What then can cause a small child to be breathing with difficulty and coughing repeatedly and why would breathing not be easy for the child as it should be? What can be done about this situation?
reference:
A caregiver who is taking care of a small child noticed that the child she is caring for is struggling to breathe, and the child's breathing is not normal.
She also noticed that the child coughs repeatedly, and the cough is very severe.
The child is not a baby that was abandoned at birth, nor a child that is usually bathed with cold water.
What then can cause a small child to be breathing with difficulty and coughing repeatedly, and why would breathing not be easy for the child as it should be? What can be done about this situation?
model_answer:
A small child with difficult breathing and repeated severe cough may have pneumonia, asthma/bronchospasm, bronchiolitis, whooping cough, or a foreign body stuck in the airway; it is not caused by being bathed with cold water or by being “abandoned at birth.”  
Breathing becomes difficult because infection or irritation can make the airways swollen, narrowed, or filled with mucus/fluid, so oxygen cannot enter the lungs properly.  
This is a danger sign: take the child urgently to the nearest hospital/clinic, especially if there is fast breathing, chest indrawing, noisy breathing, blue lips, fever, inability to drink, or unusual sleepiness.  
While going, keep the child sitting upright, avoid smoke/dust, do not force-feed, and do not give cough mixtures or antibiotics without a health worker’s assessment.  
Treatment may include oxygen, nebulized salbutamol if wheezing, antibiotics if pneumonia is suspected, suction/supportive care, or emergency removal if a foreign body is suspected.

question: A mother noticed that for the past few days, her child had started coughing continuously. At first, she thought it was a cold affecting the child's chest and that it would go away. model_answer:
Severe cough with night-time breathing difficulty in a child is commonly due to asthma/wheeze triggered by dust, smoke, cold air or infections, but it can also be from pneumonia, bronchiolitis, croup, whooping cough, tuberculosis, allergy, reflux, or a swallowed object.  
Danger signs needing urgent hospital care include fast breathing, chest indrawing, noisy breathing/wheezing/stridor, bluish lips, inability to feed or talk/cry well, severe weakness or drowsiness, persistent high fever, convulsions, dehydration, coughing blood, or worsening symptoms despite treatment.  
At the hospital, the child should be examined, oxygen level checked, and treated appropriately—often with inhaled bronchodilator for wheeze/asthma, and antibiotics only if bacterial infection such as pneumonia is suspected.  
To reduce attacks, avoid cigarette smoke, firewood/kerosene fumes, dust, strong perfumes/insecticides, cold air exposure, pets or mould if they trigger symptoms, and avoid giving random cough mixtures, leftover antibiotics, or herbal preparations.  
If the cough repeatedly wakes the child at night or comes with wheezing, the child should be reviewed for asthma and given a proper action plan and inhaler technique.

question: A man named Subero, who is 50 years old, developed a cough one day. At first, the cough was mild, but as the weeks passed and turned into months, it gradually became worse. A cough lasting 3 months with worsening breathlessness is not a “normal cough” and in Nigeria important causes include tuberculosis, chronic bronchitis/COPD from smoking or biomass smoke, asthma, pneumonia, heart failure, and less commonly lung cancer.  
The honey, hot water, bitter kola and cough syrups did not work because they may only soothe the throat but do not treat the real underlying disease if it is TB, asthma/COPD, heart disease, or another serious condition.  
He should be properly examined in hospital and have tests such as chest X-ray, sputum test/GeneXpert for TB, HIV test, oxygen level check, and possibly blood tests and spirometry.  
Treatment will depend on the result: TB needs full anti-TB drugs, asthma/COPD needs inhalers and avoidance of smoke, bacterial infection may need antibiotics, and heart-related cough needs heart treatment.  
Because he is already having difficulty breathing, he should seek care urgently, avoid self-medication, wear a mask if coughing, and return immediately if he has fever, weight loss, coughing blood, chest pain, or severe breathlessness.

question: My name is Titilola. Since yesterday, my child's body has been burning, shaving intensely. The child cannot turn their neck at all. It seems as if the child's neck can no longer be turned. Titilola, fever with severe shivering and a stiff neck in a child is a medical emergency and could be due to meningitis, severe malaria, sepsis, encephalitis, tetanus, or a deep throat/neck infection; the fact that the child can only open one eye may suggest brain/nerve involvement or serious swelling/infection.  
Do not try to force the neck to turn; take the child to the nearest hospital or emergency unit immediately, especially if there is vomiting, convulsion, confusion, weakness, rash, severe headache, or drowsiness.  
At home you can only check temperature, level of alertness, breathing, convulsions, rash, and whether the child cries with light or neck movement, but the real examination must be done by a doctor.  
In hospital, doctors may check vital signs, neck stiffness, eye/brain nerve function, do malaria test, full blood count, blood sugar, blood culture, and may do lumbar puncture to test the spinal fluid if safe.  
Possible results causing these symptoms include malaria parasites in blood, high white blood cells from infection, bacteria in blood or spinal fluid, cloudy spinal fluid with high protein/low sugar suggesting meningitis, or signs of severe infection affecting the brain or neck tissues.

question: A woman noticed that her husband coughs very strongly when he wake up in the morning while still on the bed. The cough starts suddenly and takes a long time before it stops. A woman noticed that her husband coughs very strongly when they wake up in the morning while still on the bed. The cough starts suddenly and takes a long time before it stops. What are the things that can cause death or make a person struggle to breathe severely, to the point that the person needs urgent medical attention?
What are the danger signs of breathing problems that the family should watch out for regarding cough and difficulty in breathing?
model_answer:
Severe morning cough with breathlessness can be caused by lung problems such as COPD/chronic bronchitis from smoking or indoor smoke, asthma, pneumonia, tuberculosis, lung cancer, bronchiectasis, or fluid/irritation from reflux and post-nasal drip; it can also be due to heart disease, especially heart failure where fluid collects in the lungs and causes cough and shortness of breath, worse when lying down.  
It is not only lung disease—heart disease, severe anaemia, kidney failure with fluid overload, blood clot in the lungs, severe allergic reaction, and anxiety/panic can also cause serious breathing difficulty.  
Life-threatening causes include severe asthma attack, pneumonia, TB with extensive lung damage, heart failure, pulmonary embolism, collapsed lung, heart attack, severe COVID/flu, and airway obstruction.  
Danger signs needing urgent hospital care include difficulty speaking because of breathlessness, blue lips or fingers, chest pain, fainting/confusion, very fast or noisy breathing, coughing blood, high fever, severe weakness, swelling of legs with breathlessness when lying flat, oxygen level below 92% if checked, or breathlessness that is worsening or not relieved by usual inhalers/medicines.  
He should attend hospital promptly for examination, oxygen check, chest X-ray, sputum test including TB, ECG, blood tests, and treatment based on the cause.

question: The mother of a woman who had recently given birth came to the hospital. She said that since her daughter gave birth, she has been bleeding heavily. model_answer:
Heavy bleeding a few days after delivery is an emergency called secondary postpartum haemorrhage; common causes include retained placenta or membranes, poor contraction of the womb, infection of the womb, tears in the birth canal, or rarely a bleeding disorder.  
She should be taken to hospital immediately for assessment of pulse/BP, blood level, blood grouping and cross-match, examination of the womb and birth canal, and possibly ultrasound.  
Treatment may include IV fluids, blood transfusion if anaemic or in shock, medicines to contract the womb such as oxytocin or misoprostol, antibiotics if infection is suspected, and removal of retained tissue by a skilled doctor if present.  
To regain strength she may need blood, iron/folate tablets, good nutrition, fluids, and rest, but these should not delay emergency care.  
Advise the family not to manage this at home or use herbs; return urgently for soaking pads quickly, dizziness/fainting, fever, foul-smelling discharge, severe abdominal pain, or worsening weakness.

I also noticed that he can no longer eat well as before. Whenever he wants to eat, he has to pause to catch his breath. This situation hasn't given him the chance to feed properly for about three days now.
I have already taken him to the local chemists (patent medicine stores) in our neighborhood, and they gave me some cough medicine for him because he was coughing slightly, though the cough wasn't severe. But despite all the medication he took, I noticed it didn't work. His breathing remains the same, and he still cannot eat well. Please, what kind of condition is affecting my child with this whistling breath? Also, does he need a chest examination (X-ray) to find out what is troubling him and why his chest is heaving up and down? What kind of treatment can I give this child at home to help ease his breathing so he can breathe properly? Are there other medications or alternative measures I can take for this child?
model_answer:
Your child has **danger signs of breathing difficulty**—whistling/wheezing, chest indrawing, poor feeding, and struggling to breathe—commonly from **asthma/bronchiolitis, pneumonia, or sometimes a foreign body**, and he should be seen **urgently in a hospital now**, not managed at home.  
A chest X-ray is **not always needed immediately**, but the doctor will examine him, check oxygen level, and decide if X-ray, malaria test, blood test, or other tests are necessary.  
Treatment may include **oxygen, nebulized salbutamol if wheezing, steroids if asthma-like, antibiotics if pneumonia is suspected, and fluids/feeding support** depending on the findings.  
At home while going to hospital: keep him **sitting upright**, avoid smoke/dust, give small frequent sips/feeds if he can tolerate, and use **paracetamol only if fever**, but do **not** give more cough mixtures, herbal drugs, antibiotics, or sedating medicines without prescription.  
If his lips look bluish, he becomes weak/drowsy, cannot feed at all, or breathing becomes faster/worse, treat it as an **emergency** and go to the nearest hospital immediately.

model_answer:
Heavy vaginal bleeding 6 weeks after the last period could be due to miscarriage, ectopic pregnancy, molar pregnancy, fibroids, hormonal abnormal uterine bleeding, cervical/vaginal injury or infection, bleeding disorders, or rarely cancer, so pregnancy must be assumed until tested.  
Emergency care is ABC assessment, check pulse/BP, lay her flat, give oxygen if shocked, insert two wide-bore IV lines, start normal saline/Ringer’s lactate, take blood for grouping/cross-match, and transfuse blood urgently if unstable or severely anaemic.  
Medicines that may be given early include tranexamic acid to reduce bleeding, strong pain relief, antibiotics if infection is suspected, and if miscarriage/incomplete abortion is confirmed, misoprostol or manual vacuum aspiration/D&C; oxytocin/uterotonics may be used where uterine pregnancy-related bleeding is present, while ectopic pregnancy needs urgent surgery or methotrexate only if stable and suitable.  
If she is not pregnant, treatment may include high-dose combined oral contraceptive or progesterone, tranexamic acid/NSAIDs, iron therapy, and definitive treatment for fibroids or other causes.  
Investigations include urgent urine/serum pregnancy test, full blood count, blood group/Rhesus and cross-match, clotting profile, pelvic/speculum examination, pelvic ultrasound, serum beta-hCG, infection tests as indicated, and later Pap smear/endometrial sampling if age or findings suggest cancer risk.

model_answer:
This resembles a seizure/convulsion, possibly triggered by fever, malaria, meningitis, pneumonia, or another serious infection; the stiffness, fainting, frothing/drooling, and inability to swallow are danger signs.  
Yes, it can be treated, but the child must be taken urgently to a hospital or emergency unit for assessment, malaria test, blood sugar check, temperature control, and medicines such as anti-seizure drugs, antimalarials or antibiotics if needed.  
Do not give food, water, agbo, or herbs while the child is drowsy or unable to swallow, because it can enter the lungs and cause choking or aspiration pneumonia.  
Injections should only be given by trained health workers after examining the child; using local herbs or traditional soap can delay proper treatment and may worsen the illness.  
If another convulsion occurs, lay the child on the side, remove dangerous objects, do not put anything in the mouth, and go to the hospital immediately.
